extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in research integrity, retractions, and academic publishing (general public and research community)
extracted.subtask_description: An annual editorial roundup listing the ten most-read Retraction Watch stories of the past year, with editorial choices explained and examples of notable retraction-related events and problems in scholarly publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion criterion: most-read stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Each year since 2013, we put together a roundup of the 10 most-read stories we published on the blog over the past 12 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list reflects which stories grabbed readers’ attention most; selection for this post is quantitative (most-read) rather than an editorial judgment of importance alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial selection principle: prioritize under-covered stories
rubrics_metrics.description: When other outlets are paying a lot of attention to a retraction-related story ... it’s a better use of our limited resources to focus on stories they’re missing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction Watch often chooses to report on issues that other outlets have not covered extensively, even if those are not the highest-profile items of the year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism (including false authorship attribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include a paper published in someone’s name that they hadn’t written and which plagiarized another article, and reported allegations of plagiarism by high-profile figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plagiarism and authorship misattribution are grounds for investigation, corrections, and retractions; detection may come from authors, editors, or third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabricated or falsified data
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances where an author 'faked data' in published studies and grant applications, leading to ORI findings and retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabrication/falsification triggers institutional and federal investigations (e.g., ORI), retractions of affected papers, and potential sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reuse or misrepresentation of data in grant applications
rubrics_metrics.description: A researcher admitted to reusing data in multiple grant applications while claiming the data came from different experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misrepresenting data in grant applications can result in admissions of wrongdoing and supervisory conditions on future federally funded work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of original/raw data and inability to replicate
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper was retracted after doctoral students flagged a measurement issue; the original data were lost and experiments had not been replicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of raw data and failure to reproduce results undermines the validity of findings and can be a proximate cause for retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compromised peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: A journal retracted dozens of papers with 'compromised' peer review, and its retraction notice blacklisted authors and reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compromised review processes (e.g., manipulated reviews, fake reviewers) can lead to mass retractions, author/reviewer blacklisting, and loss of indexing/impact factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal delisting and mass retractions linked to paper mills or predatory practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Nineteen Hindawi journals were removed from Clarivate’s Web of Science; Wiley retracted more than 8,000 Hindawi articles linked to paper mills and closed journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing delisting and publisher-led mass retractions are institutional responses to systemic problems like paper mills, and have broad financial and reputational consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious image/data manipulation (visual artifacts)
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper displayed an obvious pasted element (capital Ts used as error bars) on a graph; this conspicuous manipulation led to attention and retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visible signs of data/image tampering draw scrutiny and can be sufficient grounds for retraction when they indicate fabrication or careless manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books failing basic academic standards / misrepresenting primary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: A scholarly book 'fails to meet basic academic standards' and is 'filled with misinformation,' according to a scathing review, prompting further critical reviews and a published rebuttal from the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly monographs are subject to community standards; substantive errors or misrepresentation of sources can prompt public reviews and reputational consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retractions followed by replacements with softened conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: After a publisher complained, an article classifying some journals as 'predatory' was retracted and replaced with a version that softened its conclusions and language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retractions may sometimes be accompanied by corrected/republished versions that alter claims or tone; such outcomes reflect negotiations between critique and publisher response.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-generated papers with fabricated references
rubrics_metrics.description: A researcher used ChatGPT to generate a paper and posted it to a preprint server twice; the paper included fictitious references and cited non-existent works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of generative AI without verification can produce fabricated citations and text; preprint servers and editors may remove such submissions when discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community reporting and database curation
rubrics_metrics.description: If you find a retraction that’s not in The Retraction Watch Database, you can let us know here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction Watch relies on community reporting to identify and record retractions; readers are invited to submit notices or corrections to improve the database.
